description: I'm building ARES Archive around a simple idea: make exploring Mars feel hands-on, not distant. I'm interested in space science, coding, maps, and turning planetary data into experiences people can explore. I'd love to work with curious, reliable people interested in web development, UI/UX, astronomy, planetary science, GIS, data visualisation, or research. You don't need to know everything; bring ideas, initiative, and a willingness to learn together.

Its Leaflet map uses NASA Mars Trek WMTS imagery in EPSG:4326, featuring Viking MDIM 2.1 (232 m), MGS MOLA colour elevation (463 m), MOLA–HRSC hillshade (200 m), and MGS TES plagioclase mineralogy layers. The workspace also includes a Perseverance MEDA and Curiosity REMS weather dashboard, a Martian clock displaying MTC, MSD, solar longitude and rover-local solar time, and an EVA planner estimating route distance, elevation profiles, walking time, PLSS oxygen consumption, battery and thermal usage, walkback limits, and return reserves. Its EVA estimates use Tobler and Pandolf-style Earth-derived models.

AI4Mars-inspired terrain labels cover soil, bedrock, sand, and big rocks. Terrain classification and elevation are currently heuristic or simulated, not validated AI4Mars predictions or guaranteed live MOLA measurements.

details:
ARES Archive: An Interactive Mars Exploration and Mission-Planning Workspace

ARES Archive is an independent planetary exploration project designed to make the exploration of Mars more interactive, accessible, and understandable. Rather than treating Mars as a collection of distant images and scientific observations, the project brings maps, planetary data, rover telemetry, and experimental mission-planning tools into one unified workspace.

What We Developed

We developed a browser-based Mars exploration environment with three main experiences: an interactive landing page, a scientific Martian surface map, and an experimental astronaut mission planner.

The interactive map is powered by Leaflet and uses NASA Mars Trek's WMTS tile services. It supports four map products: Viking MDIM 2.1 colour imagery (232 m), MGS MOLA colour elevation (463 m), MOLA–HRSC hillshade imagery (200 m), and MGS TES plagioclase mineralogy. Users can navigate the planetary surface, inspect coordinates, explore scientific landmarks, and create custom waypoints and traverses.

Five significant locations are included: Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, and Hellas Planitia. Each has scientific context and sample exploration routes, with objectives such as core sampling, subsurface ice investigation, biosignature scanning, APXS rock chemistry, and seismic or meteorological stations.

The project also features a rover weather dashboard that attempts to retrieve observations from Perseverance's MEDA and Curiosity's REMS instruments through NASA weather feeds and an additional endpoint. A dedicated Martian clock calculates Coordinated Mars Time (MTC), Mars Sol Date (MSD), solar longitude (Ls), rover-local solar time, and mission Sol counters.

The Mission-Planning Challenge

One of our central goals was to explore how planetary mapping could connect with the practical challenges of human surface exploration. The EVA planner allows users to build astronaut traverses using custom waypoints, calculate great-circle distances, inspect elevation profiles, and estimate walking duration, oxygen consumption, suit battery and thermal usage, walkback limits, and return reserves.

Its movement and effort calculations use Tobler's hiking function and a Pandolf-style metabolic model, with adjustable assumptions for speed, terrain effort, PLSS duration, and safety reserves.

Technology and Creative Approach

The project was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Leaflet 1.9.4 for geospatial interaction. Custom JavaScript handles astronomical time calculations, weather retrieval, route geometry, terrain visualisation, and mission estimates. CSS animations, responsive layouts, interactive cards, orbital graphics, and a space-inspired interface bring the experience together.

A defining aspect of the project is its effort to distinguish measured information from estimates and simulations. AI4Mars-inspired categories represent soil, bedrock, sand, and big rocks, while the current coordinate-based classification remains heuristic rather than actual AI inference. Elevation and EVA outputs also include simulated or assumed components. Weather observations fall back to sample values when live retrieval is unavailable.

Intended Impact

ARES Archive aims to make planetary science and mission planning easier to explore through an engaging, hands-on interface. It connects orbital datasets, rover observations, geospatial technology, and simplified mission modelling to encourage curiosity about Mars, autonomous exploration, and the future challenges of human interplanetary missions.

It is an educational prototype, not an operational astronaut safety or mission-planning system. Its purpose is to turn the idea of exploring another planet into something people can investigate, experiment with, and learn from.
